divergences.reason: csharp_empty_block_style is a ReSharper-only key dotnet format does not recognise at all, but that does not make it inert: what it asks for still has to survive the IDE0055 keys dotnet format does read. Alone it does (verified: `together` alone survives). With csharp_preserve_single_line_statements = false it survives only because Curb defers to that key: dotnet format moves a statement's body, an empty `{ }` included, off its header's line, so together_same_line leaves an empty if/else/loop/using/lock/fixed/try/unsafe body where csharp_new_line_before_open_brace puts it rather than joining it (issue #131; EmptyBlockStyleTests.An_empty_statement_body_stays_off_its_header_line_when_statements_are_not_preserved). The divergence that remains appears combined with csharp_preserve_single_line_blocks = false, an IDE0055 key dotnet format does understand as 'expand every single-line block' — including the empty one Curb just recollapsed under the together opinion. The two options are in permanent, direct conflict whenever both are set this way; there is no shape Curb could choose that satisfies both at once.

For an unrecognised value, Curb falls back to the option's documented default (one_less_than_current). Measured: dotnet format's own behaviour for the same unrecognised value does not match its documented default either (it indents the label level with its statement, the no_change shape), so the two fallbacks disagree. Curb's choice — the documented default — is the more defensible of the two; dotnet format's fallback for an invalid value is undocumented.

Same fallback-mismatch shape as csharp_indent_labels: Curb falls back to the documented default (all/Allman) for an unrecognised value. Measured: dotnet format leaves the source untouched for the same unrecognised value, i.e. it silently skips applying the setting rather than falling back to its own documented default.

Not an .editorconfig key — a language-level suppression Curb honours by leaving the enclosed region unformatted, matching what IDE0055 itself would do (a suppressed analyser reports nothing, so there is nothing to fix). dotnet format whitespace is not diagnostic-driven — it is a plain Roslyn formatter pass with no concept of pragma suppression — so it always reformats the region regardless. This is a structural, permanent divergence for any suppressed region that is not already dotnet-format-clean; it is not tied to a specific option key.

Measured on a case combining indent_style = tab, tab_width = 8 and a width narrow enough to force parameter-list wrapping: dotnet format converts the outer two levels of tab indentation to four-space equivalents while leaving the wrapped argument lines as tabs, an inconsistent application of indent_style = tab that only shows up in this combination — not reproduced with indent_style = tab alone, or with reflow alone. Not fully root-caused (looks like a quirk in Roslyn's own formatter under this specific combination); recorded as observed rather than fully explained. tab_width has no dotnet format equivalent to check reflow width against outside this interaction, since dotnet format does not reflow at all.

csharp_space_after_unary_operator is a ReSharper generalized key (space_after_unary_operator) dotnet format does not recognise at all. Measured: dotnet format whitespace always normalises `- x`/`+ x`/`! x` back to `-x`/`+x`/`!x` regardless of any .editorconfig setting, since it has its own fixed, unconfigurable opinion here. Setting the key to true is a permanent, structural divergence from dotnet format for any file containing a unary expression — there is no shape Curb could pick that satisfies both dotnet format's fixed opinion and the key's own request at once.

Same permanent divergence as SpacingTests.Unary_minus_plus_and_not_take_a_space_when_asked, exercised for the two unsafe pointer prefix operators (pointer indirection `*p`, address-of `&x`) rather than unary minus/plus/not — dotnet format normalises `* p`/`& x` back to `*p`/`&x` just as unconditionally.

csharp_space_around_ternary_operator is a ReSharper generalized key (space_around_ternary_operator) dotnet format does not recognise at all. Measured: dotnet format whitespace always normalises `x > 0?x:0` back to `x > 0 ? x : 0` regardless of any .editorconfig setting — spacing around a ternary's ?/: is not configurable there. Setting the key to false is a permanent, structural divergence from dotnet format for any file containing a ternary expression.

Same permanent divergence as SpacingTests.The_ternary_operator_can_lose_its_surrounding_space, exercised on a ternary long enough to wrap under max_line_length — the wrap point itself (a SoftLine) is unaffected by the option, only the flat spacing dotnet format keeps re-adding is.

Same fallback-mismatch divergence as the dotnet-format-whitespace entry above (Curb falls back to the documented default for an unrecognised value; dotnet format's own fallback for the same invalid value disagrees), now confirmed to reproduce under a real, analyzer-driven `dotnet build -p:EnforceCodeStyleInBuild=true` too, not just the `dotnet format whitespace` CLI — expected, since IDE0055 is the same underlying Roslyn formatting engine.

Same permanent divergence as the dotnet-format-whitespace entry above (a ReSharper-only key dotnet format has no concept of, so it always normalises the space back out), now confirmed under a real `dotnet build -p:EnforceCodeStyleInBuild=true` as well as the `dotnet format whitespace` CLI.

Same permanent divergence as the dotnet-format-whitespace entry above (a ReSharper-only key dotnet format has no concept of, so it always normalises the spacing back), now confirmed under a real `dotnet build -p:EnforceCodeStyleInBuild=true` as well as the `dotnet format whitespace` CLI.

Same permanent divergence as SpacingTests.The_ternary_operator_can_lose_its_surrounding_space above, exercised on a wrapped ternary, now confirmed under a real `dotnet build -p:EnforceCodeStyleInBuild=true` as well as the `dotnet format whitespace` CLI.

Same direct conflict as the dotnet-format-whitespace entry above between csharp_empty_block_style and csharp_preserve_single_line_blocks = false, now confirmed to reproduce under a real `dotnet build -p:EnforceCodeStyleInBuild=true` as well as the `dotnet format whitespace` CLI.
Same fallback-mismatch divergence as the dotnet-format-whitespace entry above, now confirmed under a real `dotnet build -p:EnforceCodeStyleInBuild=true` as well as the `dotnet format whitespace` CLI.

Same not-fully-root-caused divergence as the dotnet-format-whitespace entry above (indent_style = tab combined with a width narrow enough to force wrapping), now confirmed to reproduce under a real `dotnet build -p:EnforceCodeStyleInBuild=true` as well as the `dotnet format whitespace` CLI.

Curb formats only the C# in a block, and leaves a block it cannot read as C# exactly as written: one holding Razor (a template, <text>, @:, a Razor comment, markup), one whose closing brace shares its line, one that never closes. The Razor engine parses Razor, so it formats them, and the markup around them. Matching it means parsing Razor, which Curb does not (#88).

The Razor engine also formats markup, directives and expressions: it re-indents element nesting, puts an @if body's brace and markup on lines of their own, normalises the spacing in @using and in an implicit expression's call, and opens a one-line @{ } out. Curb leaves everything outside a block as written until markup formatting lands (#88).

Curb keeps an indented @code or @functions line where it is and indents the block's content from that line's own column. The Razor engine moves a top-level directive block to column zero, content with it. Moving the directive's line is markup, which Curb does not format yet (#88).

The Razor engine indents by tab_width and ignores indent_size (it takes its indent from the C# options' TabSize), where dotnet format and Curb indent C# by indent_size. With indent_size = 2 and the default tab_width of 4 the engine indents a block by four.
The Razor engine adds a blank line after an #endregion that ends a @code block, before its closing brace. Curb keeps a block's last line where the formatter left it, as it does in a .cs file.
